_comment: The shared secret-masking ruleset, as data.
PLAN.md Section 25 lists this as a Build Once Contract with four call
sites: the native adapter, legacy stdout, credential handling, and the
Ansible callback bridge. The last of those is Python, which is why this
is a JSON file rather than a Go slice: one artifact, read by both
languages, so the two halves cannot drift.
HONEST STATUS: the Python half does not exist yet. Phase 22 ships this
file, the Go embed, and the COPY into the legacy runner image. Phase 25
writes the callback plugin that reads it. Saying the ruleset is applied
in Go and Python today would be a false claim, so this comment says so
instead.
There is deliberately no rule kind for a literal secret VALUE. A value
worth masking is never known at build time and must never be committed
to a file, so runtime values travel through redact.Literals instead.
That is the third channel, and it is code rather than data on purpose.
Each pattern rule carries a prefilter and samples. The prefilter is a set
of cheap lowercase substrings, at least one of which any match must
contain; a line containing none of them skips the regex entirely, which is
what keeps masking off the critical path of every log line. The samples are
strings the rule MUST mask. They exist because a wrong prefilter would
silently disable its own rule, and a silently disabled masking rule is the
worst failure this file has available: the tests assert every sample both
passes its prefilter and is actually masked, so the prefilter cannot drift
away from the pattern it guards.

rules.name: credential_field_names
rules.description: Structured-log attribute names whose value is a secret by construction. A key rule is only applicable where the attribute name is still visible, which is inside slog.HandlerOptions.ReplaceAttr and nowhere else. This is the concrete reason the ordering constraint on the logging seam exists.

rules.name: ansible_credential_field_names
rules.description: The same rule for Ansible's own variable names, which appear as attribute keys once the legacy adapter's inventory and callback output are logged.

rules.name: pem_private_key
rules.description: A PEM private key block, in any of its forms (RSA, EC, OPENSSH, PKCS8). Secret by construction: no PEM private key is ever safe to print, whether or not this process knows it is a credential. The (?s) flag lets the dot cross the newlines a PEM block always contains, and the lazy .*? stops at the first END line so two adjacent keys do not merge into one match.
samples:
-----BEGIN RSA PRIVATE KEY-----
MIIBOgIBAAJBAK
-----END RSA PRIVATE KEY-----

-----BEGIN OPENSSH PRIVATE KEY-----
b3BlbnNzaC1rZXk
-----END OPENSSH PRIVATE KEY-----

rules.name: bearer_token
rules.description: An HTTP Authorization bearer token, which reaches a log whenever a request header is dumped. Matches the scheme word too, so the masked output shows that authorization was present without showing what it was.

rules.name: json_web_token
rules.description: A JWT. The eyJ prefix is the base64url encoding of the opening of every JOSE header, so this is distinctive enough to carry almost no false-positive risk, and a JWT in a log line is a session anybody reading that line can replay.

rules.name: aws_access_key_id
rules.description: An AWS access key identifier, across the documented resource-type prefixes. The matching secret access key is deliberately NOT a pattern rule: it is 40 characters of base64 with no distinguishing prefix, so a pattern for it would scrub unrelated hashes, git object ids and base64 payloads out of every log line in the system. That value is covered by the literal channel instead, where its exact bytes are known.

rules.name: url_userinfo
rules.description: Credentials embedded in a URL, the shape a database DSN or a git remote takes. The match includes the scheme, so the masked output loses the scheme along with the credentials. That is accepted rather than worked around: RE2 has no lookbehind, so matching the userinfo alone is not expressible, and a replacement template that reassembled the surviving parts would be a place to get a leak wrong.
